q: In a year a shipper declines to declare, it may still bottle a vintage wine drawn from one property. What is that called?
opts: A tawny with an age indication
exp: The fruit comes from one estate, usually in a season judged short of a full declaration, though a few properties bottle one in declared years as well. These mature earlier and cost a fraction of a declared vintage.

q: Chilled over ice with tonic and a twist of lemon is the everyday Portuguese serve for which Port?
exp: Made from white Douro grapes in styles running dry to sweet. Treated this way it is an aperitif rather than a dessert wine, which is how most Portuguese drink it.

q: Jerez de la Frontera anchors the Sherry triangle. Which two towns complete it?
exp: El Puerto de Santa Maria and Sanlucar de Barrameda sit with Jerez in Andalucia within reach of the Atlantic, and the historic bodegas are concentrated in the three. Sanlucar's damper sea air is why its wines differ from those of Jerez.

q: A brilliant white soil that crusts over and holds winter rain through a rainless summer underpins the best Sherry vineyards. What is it called?
exp: Albariza is chalky and limestone-rich, and it sets hard after rain so that moisture is sealed beneath for the vine to draw on. Macharnudo and Balbaina are celebrated albariza pagos.

q: Nearly every dry Sherry is built on which grape?
exp: Palomino is neutral and low in acid, which suits a wine whose character is built in the bodega rather than the vineyard. Pedro Ximenez and Moscatel are kept for sweet wines.

q: A film of living yeast forms across the surface of a part-filled butt. What is it, and what does it do?
opts: Flor, which shields the wine from air
Mother, which turns the wine to vinegar
exp: Biological ageing keeps a Fino pale and gives it a dough-like, bruised-apple tang. The yeast feeds on alcohol and glycerol and leaves acetaldehyde behind.

q: Why must a wine destined to become Oloroso be fortified higher than one headed for Fino?
opts: No wine may enter a solera below seventeen percent
Flor cannot survive the higher strength
Higher alcohol makes the flor grow faster
The extra spirit is what makes the wine sweet
exp: Fino is fortified to about fifteen percent, which the yeast tolerates. Oloroso goes to seventeen or above, which kills any flor, and the wine darkens and turns nutty from oxygen instead.

q: A wine that started life under flor, lost it, and finished its ageing exposed to air is sold as what?
exp: Two lives in one glass: a Fino's saline tang beneath an oxidative, hazelnut depth. Palo Cortado is the rarer wine that arrives at the same duality by accident.

q: Which dry Sherry style may only be aged in Sanlucar de Barrameda?
exp: The cool, humid Atlantic air there keeps the flor thick through the year, so the wine stays lighter and more saline than a Fino aged inland at Jerez.

q: Wine drawn from the oldest row of casks is replaced from the row above, and so on up the stack. What is that arrangement called?
exp: Fractional blending evens out vintage differences and refreshes older wine with younger. The feeding rows are the criaderas, and no cask is ever drained completely.

q: Grapes laid out in the sun to raisin before pressing yield which near-black, syrupy Sherry?
exp: Sun-drying pushes the sugar far past what yeast can ferment, so the wine stays thick and dark. It behaves more like a sauce than a drink and is often poured over ice cream.

q: Heat is applied deliberately during the ageing of Madeira. What does it give the wine?
opts: A pale colour and softer acidity
exp: The style descends from barrels that improved while crossing the tropics as ballast. Because the wine has already been oxidised and heated, an opened bottle keeps for months.

q: Between the two ways of warming Madeira, which is reserved for the finest wines?
opts: Canteiro, years of gentle warmth in cask under the roof
Estufa, tanks held near fifty degrees for months
exp: Canteiro relies on the natural heat of the lodge and takes years. The estufa tanks do a cruder version of the same job in months, and serve everyday bottlings.

q: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual and Malmsey appear on Madeira labels. What do those names record?
opts: The number of years spent in cask
The lodge that aged the wine
exp: The four run driest to sweetest in the order Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey. Malmsey is Malvasia and the richest of them, and Sercial is bracingly dry. A wine named for one has to be made overwhelmingly from that variety.

q: Which grape accounts for most of Madeira's plantings, though it long went unmentioned on labels?
exp: Tinta Negra is a red grape adaptable enough to be made at every sweetness level. The noble white varieties together account for a small minority of the island's vines.

q: Marsala takes its name from a town on which island?
exp: The wine was developed on Sicily's western coast for the British trade in the late eighteenth century. Grillo, Catarratto and Inzolia are the main white grapes behind it.
